The session begins.

The gangplank bounces once under your boots, and then there is stone — the Lower City quay of Baldur's Gate, slick with harbour damp and loud with the end of a working day. Lanterns are coming alight along the waterfront one by one. Porters shout, a barge horn groans somewhere on the Chionthar, and above it all the city climbs in a jumble of roofs towards the dark line of the inner wall.

The cat lands beside you, tail high, and studies the quay as if it had been told to expect something.

Ahead, the passengers from your ship shuffle into a line before a trestle table under a Flaming Fist awning. A broad sergeant with an ink-stained thumb looks up from his ledger at each face. "Name. Business in the Gate. Where you'll sleep," he says, over and over, without much patience left in his voice.

To your left, on an upturned barrel by a warehouse door, a woman with quick hands fans a deck of cards. The sailors around her groan and laugh as a hand goes the wrong way. "One more seat, friend," she calls, and her eyes find you. "You look like someone who knows how to read a table."

A thin tiefling lad with a rope sling over his shoulder slips along the queue. "Carry your things up to the Lower City, ser? Cheap. Know every inn worth the name." A merchant ahead of you pulls his purse closer and steps away from him.

You have about three hundred and fifty gold, a promissory note from a man who lost the same night you won, and an order from a goddess who did not say how you would learn what she wants of you. The line moves forward. The sergeant's pen is waiting, the cards are being shuffled again, and the porter is already looking your way.

Mirela's hands don't stop. The deck riffles and bridges back into one block. "Retired," she says, as if trying the word for size, and gives you half a smile. "The seat stays warm anyway." Then she turns back to the sailors and her voice gets loud and easy again. The cat walks a wide curve around her barrel to rejoin you, and it doesn't look at her once.

The tiefling lad is at your elbow before you've finished turning. He's younger up close, sixteen maybe, with small horns filed blunt and a coat that belonged to a bigger man first.

"Tamsin, ser. Tamsin's the name." He takes in your pack, the crossbow, the cloak, and goes on fast. "A bed near the Lady, ser, yes. Only her proper house, the Lady's Hall, that's up in the Upper City, ser, behind the wall, and they've shut the gates by this hour. They won't open them for a man off a boat, not even with a good face. But..." He holds up a finger. "Down here there's the Lady's Corner, ser. It's a little shrine in the wall at the top of Cheapside, with a bowl and a stone Tymora about so tall. Dockmen toss a copper in on the way to work. And right across from it is the Three Old Kegs. Clean beds, a bar on the door, and old Nantrin doesn't let the Guild's lads drink there. Five silver a night with a fire, ser, maybe four if you don't want supper."

He smiles, quick and hopeful. "For me it's five copper to walk you up. A silver if you want me to talk the whole way. I know which streets are safe at night and which only look it." His eyes flick past you to the trestle table, where the sergeant is waving the next passenger forward. "You'll want to clear the sergeant first, ser. He asks where you're sleeping. Tell him the Kegs. He likes an answer he's heard before."

The queue moves up one more place. Tamsin puts his weight on his heels to show he'll wait.

"And who am I walking up, ser, if you don't mind me asking?"

Tamsin takes the name quickly, the way a porter takes a bag. "James, ser. Yes." He tips his head, already pleased. "A silver for the walk and the talk. I'll be right here, ser. By the bollard with the green rag on it." He goes there and leans against it like he owns the spot. The cat sits down near him and looks at him for a moment before it turns its eyes back to you.

The queue moves forward slowly. A wool merchant argues over the spelling of his own name. A family of four from upriver says "Elturel" quietly, and the sergeant's pen stops for a moment, then keeps going. It's about ten minutes before the lantern under the awning is shining on you instead of on the back of someone's head.

Up close, Sergeant Brannick is thick through the neck and tired around the eyes. Ink has worked into the cracks of his knuckles. He doesn't look up until you've finished, and then he looks at you longer than he looked at anyone else.

"Zaranda's." He grunts, and it might be respect. "You'll know how this goes, then." He writes in the big ledger in a heavy square hand: *Worgen, James. Tethyr. Work. Three Old Kegs.* "Work. What kind. Sword?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. "Fist's hiring. Silver a day, bed and bread, at the Seatower. They don't ask much. Worth knowing." He blots the line with his sleeve.

Then, without hurrying and without hiding it, he pulls a scrap of paper from under the ledger's cover. He copies something onto it in a few quick strokes and folds it in half twice. He doesn't call for anyone. A boy of nine or ten in a cap too big for him comes out of the shadow of the warehouse wall, takes the scrap from between the sergeant's fingers and is gone up the landing stair into the streets, bare feet slapping on the wet stone.

Brannick has already turned his eyes past your shoulder. "Next."

Over by the bollard, the cat has stood up. It isn't watching the boy. It faces uphill, toward the crowded roofs above the quay, very still, with one forepaw lifted off the stones, like something up there is pulling at it.

Brannick doesn't look up right away. He finishes the stroke he started, sets the pen down across the ledger, and only then raises his eyes. He glances once down the queue, then back at you.

"Not Fist," he says, just as quietly. "Nobody at the Seatower wants you."

He rubs his inky thumb against his finger as if he could get the ink out.

"Some names go up the hill. Always have. Yours is one." He shrugs, a small movement in that thick neck. "Not my business why. Not trouble, far as I know. People up there don't send trouble down an alley. They send a man in a good coat."

He studies your face for a moment, the way he'd look over a recruit's boots.

"You owe anybody up there, Zaranda's?"

Behind you the wool merchant clears his throat loudly. Down by the bollard, Tamsin is pretending not to watch. The cat hasn't moved. It's still facing the roofs.

Brannick's mouth moves at one corner. It's the closest he has come to a smile all night.

"Copper's cheap," he says. "Bowl's on your way up. The lad'll show you."

Then the half-smile is gone. He doesn't lean in, and his voice doesn't drop any further. He just says it flat, like he's reading back a ledger line.

"Nobody left it tonight. It's on a list. The list's older than your boat." He taps the closed cover of the ledger once with his inky thumb. "I don't say whose. Not on a quay, with half the boat behind you. Somebody wants to know when you land, and now they know. That's all it is. If it were worse, I'd tell you to take the Fist's silver and sleep in the Seatower."

He picks the pen back up, and that settles it.

"Kegs is a good bed. Stay there a night or two, and whoever it is comes to you." His eyes go past your shoulder. "Next."

The wool merchant pushes forward before you've fully stepped aside, already spelling his name out loud.

Down by the bollard with the green rag, Tamsin straightens up as you turn, and he hitches the rope sling higher on his shoulder. The cat is still sitting beside him, facing up the hill. When you come closer it gives a single flick of its tail, but it doesn't turn around. Beyond the landing stair, the barefoot boy and his slip are long gone among the lanterns and the wet roofs.

Tamsin is waiting to take you up. Nothing else on the quay needs you tonight unless you want it to.

James presses the silver into Tamsin's palm. The boy closes his fingers on it fast and tucks it inside the big coat, somewhere near his ribs. "Thank you, ser. Shrine first, ser, yes. This way."

The landing stair is steep and worn hollow in the middle. At the top the quay noise drops behind you, and the Lower City closes in: tall narrow houses leaning over the street, shutters closed, a lantern every forty or fifty feet and dark between them. Tamsin walks half a pace ahead and keeps to the middle of the street. After the first turning, the cat runs on ahead of you both without being asked and stays there, tail up, heading uphill.

At your question Tamsin glances back at you once, then down at the cobbles.

"Who pays, ser?" He laughs a little, too quickly. "Everybody pays for something in the Gate, ser. Moneylenders, mostly. A man skips out on a loan in Waterdeep, comes home on a boat, and someone on Bloomridge wants to know the hour he lands. Then the Guild likes to know who comes off with a heavy purse and nobody meeting him. The lads on the quay have eyes for that, ser." His hand goes to the rope sling and adjusts it, though it hadn't slipped. "And the old houses up the hill keep stewards, and the stewards keep a sergeant or two. Everybody knows that, ser. Nobody says it."

He walks on for a few steps before he adds, more quietly, "Not that I'd know who buys which, ser."

He talks faster for a while after that. This alley is fine by day, but you don't go into it at night. A cutpurse works the steps by the chandler's, so keep your purse on the wall side. The bakehouse on the corner sells yesterday's bread at half price before dawn. The street widens and starts to climb harder. That's Cheapside, he says, all stalls by day, shut up now under canvas and rope.

Near the top, the cat stops at a side lane and sits down in the middle of it.

It faces down the lane, not up the street. At the far end a big building stands dark against the sky, a block of pale stone much heavier than the houses around it, with no light in any of its windows except one small one low down near the ground. The cat's ears are flat forward.

"Counting House, ser," Tamsin says, following your eyes. "That's where the money sleeps. Half the gold in the Lower City's in there, and the Fist walks round it twice an hour." He looks at the low lit window a moment longer than he needs to, then turns away. "Not our road, ser. Here."

Ten feet on, a niche is set into the corner wall at the head of Cheapside: a stone Tymora about two feet tall, her face rubbed smooth by many hands, one arm raised with a coin in its fingers. In front of her is a shallow bronze bowl, green at the rim, with a scatter of coppers in the bottom and a stub of candle burning in a jar beside it. Across the street, a lamp hangs over a door with three barrel-ends nailed above it. Under the lamp is a bar-slot, and there's a yellow glow behind the shutters. That's the Three Old Kegs.

The cat has come up behind you. It doesn't look at the shrine. It sits with its back to the stone Lady and faces down the lane again, toward the dark bulk of the Counting House.

"There's the Lady, ser, and there's your bed," Tamsin says. "Nantrin's still up. He always is."

The bowl is right in front of you, and the inn door is twenty feet away. Nothing else is calling for you tonight unless you want it to.

The copper rings once on the bronze. It doesn't settle with the others. It runs around the curve of the bowl in a tight little circle, slows, and comes to rest against the rim on the far side, tipped up on its edge against the green metal. It leans toward the lane. The other coppers lie flat. The bowl might sit a little crooked in its niche. It's hard to tell by candlelight.

The stone under your fingers is cool and smooth, worn down by a lot of other hands. Nobody answers. The candle stub ducks once in its jar and stands up again.

You crouch down beside the cat. It doesn't look at you, but when you reach for it through the bond it opens up at once, the way it does when it has been waiting to be asked.

The world goes grey and sharp and close to the ground. The lane runs out ahead in cobbles as big as paving slabs, and every crack in them is clear in the dark. The smells come in layers: cold tallow from the candle, piss in the gutter, the bakehouse's old ovens, and under it all the harbour, much stronger than your own nose ever gets it. Down the lane, the pale block of the Counting House fills the end of the street. Its one low window is a hot yellow square. A shadow crosses the lamp inside once, bent over, and then crosses back.

But the window isn't what the cat wants you to see. Its attention runs along the ground, and halfway down the lane there's an iron grate set in the gutter. A thread of air comes up out of it that is colder than the street. It smells of wet stone, and salt, and very old metal.

Then there is the feeling under all of it, and the cat has no picture for it. It's a *pull*, downward and under, like a mouse scratching behind a wall where no paw can reach. The cat wants it badly, and it wants nothing to do with it. Both feelings come through at once, strong enough that the fur on its spine lifts, and you feel that in your own shoulders.

Then the link loosens and you're back in your own eyes, crouched on the cobbles with your knees aching. The cat is sitting exactly as it was, tail wrapped tight around its feet.

Behind you, Tamsin has stayed. He's standing a few feet back with his thumbs hooked in the rope sling. He's been watching a grown man crouch in the street and stare down a dark lane with his cat, and he's polite enough not to ask about it.

"Cats don't like that lane, ser," he offers. "Never have. Folk say there's rats under the Counting House big as dogs, from all the old cellars." He glances at the low window again, quickly, and then makes himself look at the inn door. "Nantrin'll bar up soon, ser. Is there anything else you'll want of me tonight?"

Tamsin answers too quickly.

"Cleaners, ser." He shrugs inside the big coat. "The Counting House pays folk to scrub the floors at night, when the money's asleep. Somebody has to do the stairs, ser. That's all the window is." He looks at the inn door again, not at you. "I just look at lights, ser. Bad habit. Nantrin says I'll walk into a cart one day."

He doesn't say whether he knows the person behind the window, and he doesn't look down the lane again. His thumbs come out of the rope sling, and he puts them back, more carefully this time.

When you tell him he doesn't owe you an answer, he stops for a moment. He seems to be deciding whether that's a kindness or a trap. He settles on kindness, though he doesn't trust it all the way.

"Thank you, ser." Then he goes straight back to business, the way you'd step back onto solid ground. "If you need anything carried tomorrow, or need to find someone, or want to know what a thing ought to cost before some Calishite charges you double, I'm at the quay from first light, ser. Green rag bollard. Ask anybody for Tamsin." He steps back toward Cheapside. "Good night, ser. Mind the cat in that lane."

Across the street, the bar-slot under the Three Old Kegs' lamp scrapes open. A pair of old eyes looks out at the empty street, at you, at the cat, and then the slot stays open, waiting. Inside, someone is dragging a bench across the floorboards.

The cat hasn't moved. It still sits with its back to the stone Lady and its face to the dark lane, tail wrapped tight around its feet.

Nantrin is waiting at the slot. Nothing else is going to happen out here tonight unless you want it to.

"Good night, ser," Tamsin says. He's already going. He takes Cheapside at a trot with the rope sling bouncing on his back, and the dark between the lanterns swallows him before the first corner.

The cat takes longer. When you beckon, it gets up, but it looks down the lane one more time before it follows. Then it crosses the street at your heel, close enough that its fur brushes your boot.

The old eyes at the bar-slot take in your face, the crossbow and the cat, and then the slot snaps shut. A bar scrapes in its brackets. A bolt goes, then a second one, and the door opens just wide enough for a man and a cat.

Nantrin is small and bent, and he must be seventy. He has a bald head with a white fringe and a leather apron over a nightshirt, and there's a poker in his hand that he isn't trying to hide. He looks you up and down once more in the light, then steps back to let you in.

"Tamsin." He says it as if he's checking a delivery against the docket. "Boy sends me the quiet ones. Come in before you let the night in."

The common room is low and warm and smells of woodsmoke and spilled ale that has been scrubbed up. There are four tables. The benches are up on three of them, and the one he was dragging stands crooked by the hearth, where a fire has burned down to a red bed. Three barrels with brass taps sit on a trestle behind the bar. Under the bar something stirs: a fat grey tabby with a torn ear. It opens one yellow eye at your cat and makes a low noise in its throat that isn't quite a growl.

Your cat ignores her. It doesn't go to the fire. It walks straight to the window shutter that faces the street, the side where the lane is, and sits down under it, looking up at the slats.

"That's Brick," Nantrin says, nodding at the tabby. "She was here first. Yours keeps to his side, she'll keep to hers." He sets the poker against the hearth and shoots the bolts home behind you, one, two, then drops the bar. "A room, yes. Top of the stair, back of the house, a bed with no fleas and a bolt on the inside. Fire's extra wood, I'll bring it up. Supper's what's left this hour: pease pottage still warm in the pot, end of a loaf, bit of cheese. Five silver the lot, four without the eating." He holds out a dry, lined palm, not pushy about it, just the way he's done it for forty years. "In the hand before the stair. Breakfast's at first light, and that's in the price."

He glances at your cat under the shutter, then back at you.

"Supper, then?"

Nantrin counts the five silver on his palm with one crooked finger, the way he'd count bolts of cloth off a cart, and closes his hand.

"Five." He drops them into his apron pocket. "Water for the cat. Sit."

He takes the bench he'd been dragging, sets it square by the hearth with a knock, and goes behind the bar. You hear an iron pot lid, a ladle scraping the bottom, a knife on a board. He comes back with a wooden bowl of pease pottage, thick and grey-green with a skin on it. There's a heel of brown loaf on the rim and a wedge of hard yellow cheese, and he puts a chipped saucer of water on the floor without bending more than he has to. He adds a split log to the embers, and it catches slowly, hissing at one end.

The pottage is better than it looks. It's salty, with a bit of ham bone somewhere in it.

The cat doesn't come to the saucer. It stays under the shutter. Brick slides out from under the bar, sniffs the water, decides it isn't hers, and goes back.

Nantrin takes the stool across the hearth from you and lowers himself onto it one joint at a time. He thinks about your question before he answers.

"House. Bar goes on at midnight, comes off at first light. That's now, near enough." He jerks his chin at the door. "I don't lift it in between. Not for the Fist, not for a man bleeding, not for my own sister, and she's tried. Anybody wants you in the night can knock till his knuckles go, and he can come back at breakfast."

He holds up a second finger.

"Callers by day wait down here. They don't go up my stair. Nobody does unless he's paid for the bed at the top of it. I come up and knock, and you come down or you don't. I don't say who's in the house. If someone asks, I say I keep an inn, not a list."

A third finger, and a sniff.

"Guild lads drink elsewhere. If one comes in polite, he gets told polite. If he comes in otherwise..." He looks at the poker against the hearthstones, and that's the rest of the sentence.

He watches the log burn for a moment.

"Somebody looking for you." It isn't a question. He looks at the crossbow propped by your knee, then at the cat under the window. "Most that come off a boat and say that are waiting on money or running from it. Don't tell me which. Just don't bring it through my door bleeding."

Then he pushes himself up off the stool, takes the poker, and goes to look at the bar across the door, though it hasn't moved. On the way back he stops beside your cat. It's still sitting under the shutter, face turned up to the slats on the lane side, and the tip of its tail is twitching.

"Yours wants out," Nantrin says. "There's a cat-flap in the scullery wall, low by the drain. Brick uses it. It's a cat's business where it goes at night, not mine." He puts the poker back in its place. "Room's top of the stair, at the back. Fire's laid. Bolt's on your side."

He goes behind the bar and starts wiping down a tap that's already clean. That's how an old man stays up without having to say he's waiting for you to finish.

The pottage is still warm, the log has caught properly, and the stair is there whenever you want it. Nothing else will happen tonight unless you want it to.

The cat is off the floor before you've finished the thought. It looks back at you once from the scullery doorway, and its tail goes straight up. Brick watches from under the bar with one yellow eye. When the flap knocks shut behind your cat, she shuts the eye again. Somebody else's cat using her door is not worth getting up for.

The link opens as easily as it did before.

The street comes up grey and sharp. The cat crosses it low and quick, past the Lady's niche. The candle stub has burned down another finger's width, and in the bowl your copper still stands on its edge against the far rim. The cat doesn't stop for it. It turns into the lane and goes along the wall side, the same way Tamsin told you to carry your purse.

The grate is about thirty paces in, ninety feet or so from where you're sitting by the hearth. The link is still clear there, but you can feel the far edge of it, the way you feel the end of a rope you're paying out. The Counting House waits at the end of the lane with its one hot yellow window, and that's farther than the bond reaches. The cat seems to know it. It stops at the grate and doesn't go a step past.

It puts its nose to the bars.

The cold air comes straight up into its face. Below the iron there is a shaft of old brick, square and slimed, dropping maybe fifteen feet. At the bottom, black water moves. It doesn't run like a drain. It lifts and settles, lifts and settles, slapping softly against the brick, slow as breathing. Salt, wet stone, and under them the old metal again, stronger here, like the smell left on your fingers from a purse of coppers that has been handled a long time.

Then there's something the cat didn't show you the first time. Just under the lip of the grate, an iron staple is driven into the brickwork, and a rope is tied to it. It's good hemp, tarred, knotted every arm's length. It hangs down the shaft and into the black water, and the end is under the surface. The cat's nose goes to it without being asked. Tar. Fish-oil. A man's sweat, sharp and fresh, a day or two old at most. Somebody has been down there, and he didn't take his rope up after him.

The pull doesn't come from the shaft, though. The cat makes that clear without having the words for it. The water at the bottom is only water. What it wants is beyond the water and below it, off to the side, toward the end of the lane where the Counting House stands. It's deep. *Wrong.* Under that *wrong*, the same hungry wanting as before. Its claws flex on the bars, and you feel how much it wants to slip between them. It doesn't. You told it not to.

Light comes swinging round the far end of the lane.

The cat is off the grate and flat in a doorway's shadow before you've registered the sound of boots. Two Flaming Fist men come up from the Counting House corner with a lantern on a pole, in red-and-orange, walking at the pace of men who have done this circuit too many times tonight. The lantern swings over the grate and doesn't stop there. Neither of them looks down.

"...twice an hour, and for what," one says. "Nobody's carrying a strongroom off through the gutter."

"Keep walking," says the other.

They pass the doorway within six feet. The cat's heart is going fast and light, and it doesn't move until the lantern has turned up Cheapside and gone. Then it creeps back to the grate's edge and sits there with its tail wrapped tight. The rope hangs in the shaft. The water breathes at the bottom.

It turns its head and looks back up the lane toward the Kegs. It's waiting for you.

At the corner of the side lane it stops for a moment and looks down towards the pale bulk of the Counting House. By day the place is all open shutters and clerks on the steps. Then it turns and comes on without being called.

At the bottom of Cheapside a crier in a stained blue coat is standing on a mounting block with a bundle of broadsheets under one arm. He's shouting the same lines over and over to anyone who'll slow down.

"*Baldur's Mouth!* Third this season! Drowned man off the Grey Harbour steps at dawn, and a copper in his teeth! Umberlee's sisters say it's no offering of theirs! The Fist says it's no murder of theirs! *Baldur's Mouth*, two copper, read who's paying the sea!"

A couple of dockmen buy a sheet and argue over it as they walk off. One of them says the sea takes what it's owed. The other says the sea doesn't pay coppers, people do.

East along the inside of the outer wall the crowd thins. There are fewer stalls and more warehouses here, and the air smells of dung and hot iron instead of fish. The Basilisk Gate is just as Nantrin described it: a deep, dark arch with a stone lizard crouched over it. Half its head and one foreleg have broken away, so it looks more like a sleeping dog than a basilisk. Two Flaming Fist men on the gate are going through a farmer's turnip cart for no reason anyone can see. One of them glances at James's crossbow and then at the cat, decides neither is a turnip, and waves him through with two fingers.

Outside the wall the city doesn't stop. It just stops being tidy. The road out from the gate is mud and straw, lined on both sides by fenced yards full of wagons, axle-trees, mules and men shouting about axles. James asks the first carter he sees for Hesk's. The man points with his whip, three yards along on the left, and adds without being asked, "Tell her I'll have it Highharvestide."

Hesk's yard has a painted board over the gate, HESK — CARTAGE — BREWERS & GENERAL, and the paint is newer than the board. Inside is a packed-earth yard with two big drays and a lighter wagon, a long stable along one side with mules' heads looking out over the half-doors, and a house of whitewashed brick at the back. A tall, heavy-shouldered woman of about fifty stands in the middle of it with her sleeves rolled to the elbow and a slate in one hand. She is telling a young drayman exactly how much a cracked barrel costs and who will be paying for it.

"...six silver for the cask, and the beer's on top, and it's coming out of yours, not mine." She looks up at James, takes in the cloak, the crossbow and the cat in one sweep, and goes straight to business. "If you're hiring, the light wagon's free from noon. If you're owing, you're early, and I'll take it."

Before James can answer, a voice comes from the stable, slow and low, plainly talking to a mule. "No, you don't. Stand. *Stand.* There's a good lass."

A man ducks out under the half-door with a hoof-pick in his hand. He's lean and bandy-legged, somewhere past fifty, with a grey beard cropped short and a face the road has turned to leather. He's wiping his hands down his apron when he sees James, and his hands stop.

Dace Rook looks at him for a long moment. He looks at James's face, then at his hands, then at the cat. Then he looks back at the hands again.

"Well," he says. "Corra said you'd turn up if you were ever this far north." He doesn't come any closer yet. The hoof-pick hangs from his fingers. "You come to eat, James, or you come for your money?"

Orla Hesk has stopped talking to the drayman. She's watching the two of them over her slate.

As I take my seat, I ask Nantrin quietly, “Heard a caller in the night. Did he leave a name or a message?”

“Thank you for keeping him downstairs.”

Over breakfast, I ask, “An old friend of mine, Dace Rook, bought into a carter’s yard outside the Basilisk Gate. Do you know it? I’d like to pay him a visit this morning.”

“If he returns, he can leave a name and a message. No need to tell him where I’ve gone.”

I finish breakfast, thank Nantrin, and head for Hesk’s yard with the cat, following his directions to the Basilisk Gate.

The strongest part was the atmosphere. The quay, Nantrin’s inn, and Hesk’s yard felt inhabited rather than staged for James. Tamsin’s nervous politeness, Brannick’s guarded professionalism, and Nantrin’s firm house rules gave me people I wanted to talk to. Corra’s letter was the highlight: affectionate, practical, and gently damning about James’s gambling. It gave me a reason to visit Dace beyond collecting money.

The cat worked very well as a patron’s instrument. Its conflicting attraction and fear made the Counting House intriguing without simply delivering instructions. Scouting the grate produced useful facts—distance, rope, water, patrol—while respecting the limit I set. That felt like information I could eventually build a plan around.

**What broke**
- The starting records weren’t reconciled with the campaign files. The missing letter interrupted a good scene, especially when I was initially asked to invent something explicitly left to the GM. The correction was gracious, and the resulting letter was excellent.
- There were other sheet discrepancies: Arcana became History, the rapier lost its established proficiency, and the rod and cloak required attunement despite the campaign override. These didn’t affect a roll today, but they undermine confidence in later mechanical play.
- One combined out-of-game correction and in-character action returned “The question could not be sent.” I can’t diagnose that, but it broke the flow.

**What was missing**
A little more momentum and room for initiative from NPCs. I enjoyed choosing to visit Dace, but many turns ended with some version of “nothing else will happen unless you want it to.” Repeated that often, it made the city feel less independent than the descriptions suggested. Likewise, reminders that breakfast was waiting started to feel like nudges to stop investigating.

The mystery has strong ingredients, but I’m ready for an actionable proposition soon: someone who wants something, an opportunity with a deadline, or a concrete lead James can pursue. Not the big reveal yet—just enough to begin making consequential choices toward the crew-and-heist campaign.

Overall, I wanted to keep playing. Preserve the character work and careful scouting, clean up the records, and let the world push back a little more.

Yes—at the grate. I wanted to investigate the rope and work out where the water led, perhaps by going outside myself. But Nantrin had just explained that the inn was barred for the night, and the cat felt both drawn to and frightened by something below. I chose not to turn a first look into a solo dungeon entry.

That restraint felt good: I had discovered a possible approach worth returning to with preparation.

There was also a smaller moment with Tamsin. I wanted to press him about the lit window, but James had explicitly offered him permission not to answer. When he dodged, I let him go. I’m still curious whether someone he cares about works there.

My eyes linger on the cards a moment too long. “Retired,” I tell the woman, and turn to the tiefling lad.

“I can carry my kit, but I’ll pay for a guide. What’s your name, and what would you charge to find me a decent bed near a shrine of Tymora? Somewhere I can sleep without keeping one eye on my boots.”
turns.reply:
Mirela's hands don't stop. The deck riffles and bridges back into one block. "Retired," she says, as if trying the word for size, and gives you half a smile. "The seat stays warm anyway." Then she turns back to the sailors and her voice gets loud and easy again. The cat walks a wide curve around her barrel to rejoin you, and it doesn't look at her once.

The tiefling lad is at your elbow before you've finished turning. He's younger up close, sixteen maybe, with small horns filed blunt and a coat that belonged to a bigger man first.

"Tamsin, ser. Tamsin's the name." He takes in your pack, the crossbow, the cloak, and goes on fast. "A bed near the Lady, ser, yes. Only her proper house, the Lady's Hall, that's up in the Upper City, ser, behind the wall, and they've shut the gates by this hour. They won't open them for a man off a boat, not even with a good face. But..." He holds up a finger. "Down here there's the Lady's Corner, ser. It's a little shrine in the wall at the top of Cheapside, with a bowl and a stone Tymora about so tall. Dockmen toss a copper in on the way to work. And right across from it is the Three Old Kegs. Clean beds, a bar on the door, and old Nantrin doesn't let the Guild's lads drink there. Five silver a night with a fire, ser, maybe four if you don't want supper."

He smiles, quick and hopeful. "For me it's five copper to walk you up. A silver if you want me to talk the whole way. I know which streets are safe at night and which only look it." His eyes flick past you to the trestle table, where the sergeant is waving the next passenger forward. "You'll want to clear the sergeant first, ser. He asks where you're sleeping. Tell him the Kegs. He likes an answer he's heard before."

The queue moves up one more place. Tamsin puts his weight on his heels to show he'll wait.

"And who am I walking up, ser, if you don't mind me asking?"

By the bollard with the green rag on it." He goes there and leans against it like he owns the spot. The cat sits down near him and looks at him for a moment before it turns its eyes back to you.

The queue moves forward slowly. A wool merchant argues over the spelling of his own name. A family of four from upriver says "Elturel" quietly, and the sergeant's pen stops for a moment, then keeps going. It's about ten minutes before the lantern under the awning is shining on you instead of on the back of someone's head.

Up close, Sergeant Brannick is thick through the neck and tired around the eyes. Ink has worked into the cracks of his knuckles. He doesn't look up until you've finished, and then he looks at you longer than he looked at anyone else.

"Zaranda's." He grunts, and it might be respect. "You'll know how this goes, then." He writes in the big ledger in a heavy square hand: *Worgen, James. Tethyr. Work. Three Old Kegs.* "Work. What kind. Sword?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. "Fist's hiring. Silver a day, bed and bread, at the Seatower. They don't ask much. Worth knowing." He blots the line with his sleeve.

Then, without hurrying and without hiding it, he pulls a scrap of paper from under the ledger's cover. He copies something onto it in a few quick strokes and folds it in half twice. He doesn't call for anyone. turns.message:
I join Tamsin and hand him the promised silver. “Lead on. Shrine first, then the Kegs.”

As we leave the quay, I ask, “Who usually pays for news of arrivals, Tamsin? Besides jealous wives and creditors.”
turns.reply:
James presses the silver into Tamsin's palm. The boy closes his fingers on it fast and tucks it inside the big coat, somewhere near his ribs. "Thank you, ser. Shrine first, ser, yes. This way."

The landing stair is steep and worn hollow in the middle. At the top the quay noise drops behind you, and the Lower City closes in: tall narrow houses leaning over the street, shutters closed, a lantern every forty or fifty feet and dark between them. Tamsin walks half a pace ahead and keeps to the middle of the street. After the first turning, the cat runs on ahead of you both without being asked and stays there, tail up, heading uphill.

At your question Tamsin glances back at you once, then down at the cobbles.

"Who pays, ser?" He laughs a little, too quickly. "Everybody pays for something in the Gate, ser. Moneylenders, mostly. A man skips out on a loan in Waterdeep, comes home on a boat, and someone on Bloomridge wants to know the hour he lands. Then the Guild likes to know who comes off with a heavy purse and nobody meeting him. The lads on the quay have eyes for that, ser." His hand goes to the rope sling and adjusts it, though it hadn't slipped. "And the old houses up the hill keep stewards, and the stewards keep a sergeant or two. Everybody knows that, ser. Nobody says it."

He walks on for a few steps before he adds, more quietly, "Not that I'd know who buys which, ser."

He talks faster for a while after that. This alley is fine by day, but you don't go into it at night. A cutpurse works the steps by the chandler's, so keep your purse on the wall side. The bakehouse on the corner sells yesterday's bread at half price before dawn. The street widens and starts to climb harder. That's Cheapside, he says, all stalls by day, shut up now under canvas and rope.

Near the top, the cat stops at a side lane and sits down in the middle of it.

It faces down the lane, not up the street. At the far end a big building stands dark against the sky, a block of pale stone much heavier than the houses around it, with no light in any of its windows except one small one low down near the ground. The cat's ears are flat forward.

"Counting House, ser," Tamsin says, following your eyes. "That's where the money sleeps. Half the gold in the Lower City's in there, and the Fist walks round it twice an hour." He looks at the low lit window a moment longer than he needs to, then turns away. "Not our road, ser. Here."

Ten feet on, a niche is set into the corner wall at the head of Cheapside: a stone Tymora about two feet tall, her face rubbed smooth by many hands, one arm raised with a coin in its fingers. In front of her is a shallow bronze bowl, green at the rim, with a scatter of coppers in the bottom and a stub of candle burning in a jar beside it. Across the street, a lamp hangs over a door with three barrel-ends nailed above it. Under the lamp is a bar-slot, and there's a yellow glow behind the shutters. That's the Three Old Kegs.

The cat has come up behind you. It doesn't look at the shrine. It sits with its back to the stone Lady and faces down the lane again, toward the dark bulk of the Counting House.

"There's the Lady, ser, and there's your bed," Tamsin says. "Nantrin's still up. He always is."

The bowl is right in front of you, and the inn door is twenty feet away. Nothing else is calling for you tonight unless you want it to.

turns.message:
I drop a copper into the bowl and rest my fingers against the worn stone.

“Made it,” I murmur. “I’d appreciate clearer instructions than last time.”

Then I crouch beside the cat, looking down the lane with it, and reach out through our familiar bond: *Something in the Counting House? Show me what you can.*
turns.reply:
The copper rings once on the bronze. It doesn't settle with the others. It runs around the curve of the bowl in a tight little circle, slows, and comes to rest against the rim on the far side, tipped up on its edge against the green metal. It leans toward the lane. The other coppers lie flat. The bowl might sit a little crooked in its niche. It's hard to tell by candlelight.

The stone under your fingers is cool and smooth, worn down by a lot of other hands. Nobody answers. The candle stub ducks once in its jar and stands up again.

You crouch down beside the cat. It doesn't look at you, but when you reach for it through the bond it opens up at once, the way it does when it has been waiting to be asked.

The world goes grey and sharp and close to the ground. The lane runs out ahead in cobbles as big as paving slabs, and every crack in them is clear in the dark. The smells come in layers: cold tallow from the candle, piss in the gutter, the bakehouse's old ovens, and under it all the harbour, much stronger than your own nose ever gets it. Down the lane, the pale block of the Counting House fills the end of the street. Its one low window is a hot yellow square. A shadow crosses the lamp inside once, bent over, and then crosses back.

But the window isn't what the cat wants you to see. Its attention runs along the ground, and halfway down the lane there's an iron grate set in the gutter. A thread of air comes up out of it that is colder than the street. It smells of wet stone, and salt, and very old metal.

Then there is the feeling under all of it, and the cat has no picture for it. It's a *pull*, downward and under, like a mouse scratching behind a wall where no paw can reach. The cat wants it badly, and it wants nothing to do with it. Both feelings come through at once, strong enough that the fur on its spine lifts, and you feel that in your own shoulders.

Then the link loosens and you're back in your own eyes, crouched on the cobbles with your knees aching. The cat is sitting exactly as it was, tail wrapped tight around its feet.

Behind you, Tamsin has stayed. He's standing a few feet back with his thumbs hooked in the rope sling. He's been watching a grown man crouch in the street and stare down a dark lane with his cat, and he's polite enough not to ask about it.

"Cats don't like that lane, ser," he offers. "Never have. Folk say there's rats under the Counting House big as dogs, from all the old cellars." He glances at the low window again, quickly, and then makes himself look at the inn door. "Nantrin'll bar up soon, ser. Is there anything else you'll want of me tonight?"

“Good night, Tamsin.”

I beckon the cat and cross to the inn. “James Worgen. Tamsin recommended you for a clean bed and supper. Have you room for me and a well-mannered cat?”
turns.reply:
"Good night, ser," Tamsin says. He's already going. He takes Cheapside at a trot with the rope sling bouncing on his back, and the dark between the lanterns swallows him before the first corner.

The cat takes longer. When you beckon, it gets up, but it looks down the lane one more time before it follows. Then it crosses the street at your heel, close enough that its fur brushes your boot.

The old eyes at the bar-slot take in your face, the crossbow and the cat, and then the slot snaps shut. A bar scrapes in its brackets. A bolt goes, then a second one, and the door opens just wide enough for a man and a cat.

Nantrin is small and bent, and he must be seventy. He has a bald head with a white fringe and a leather apron over a nightshirt, and there's a poker in his hand that he isn't trying to hide. He looks you up and down once more in the light, then steps back to let you in.

"Tamsin." He says it as if he's checking a delivery against the docket. "Boy sends me the quiet ones. Come in before you let the night in."

The common room is low and warm and smells of woodsmoke and spilled ale that has been scrubbed up. There are four tables. The benches are up on three of them, and the one he was dragging stands crooked by the hearth, where a fire has burned down to a red bed. Three barrels with brass taps sit on a trestle behind the bar. Under the bar something stirs: a fat grey tabby with a torn ear. It opens one yellow eye at your cat and makes a low noise in its throat that isn't quite a growl.

Your cat ignores her. It doesn't go to the fire. It walks straight to the window shutter that faces the street, the side where the lane is, and sits down under it, looking up at the slats.

"That's Brick," Nantrin says, nodding at the tabby. "She was here first. Yours keeps to his side, she'll keep to hers." He sets the poker against the hearth and shoots the bolts home behind you, one, two, then drops the bar. "A room, yes. Top of the stair, back of the house, a bed with no fleas and a bolt on the inside. Fire's extra wood, I'll bring it up. Supper's what's left this hour: pease pottage still warm in the pot, end of a loaf, bit of cheese. Five silver the lot, four without the eating." He holds out a dry, lined palm, not pushy about it, just the way he's done it for forty years. "In the hand before the stair. Breakfast's at first light, and that's in the price."

He glances at your cat under the shutter, then back at you.

"Supper, then?"

“Supper, gladly.” I count five silver into his hand. “And a little water for the cat, if you please.”

As I settle near the hearth, I ask, “Anything I should know about the house? Callers, closing hours—that sort of thing. I may have someone looking for me tomorrow.”
turns.reply:
Nantrin counts the five silver on his palm with one crooked finger, the way he'd count bolts of cloth off a cart, and closes his hand.

"Five." He drops them into his apron pocket. "Water for the cat. Sit."

He takes the bench he'd been dragging, sets it square by the hearth with a knock, and goes behind the bar. You hear an iron pot lid, a ladle scraping the bottom, a knife on a board. He comes back with a wooden bowl of pease pottage, thick and grey-green with a skin on it. There's a heel of brown loaf on the rim and a wedge of hard yellow cheese, and he puts a chipped saucer of water on the floor without bending more than he has to. He adds a split log to the embers, and it catches slowly, hissing at one end.

The pottage is better than it looks. It's salty, with a bit of ham bone somewhere in it.

The cat doesn't come to the saucer. It stays under the shutter. Brick slides out from under the bar, sniffs the water, decides it isn't hers, and goes back.

Nantrin takes the stool across the hearth from you and lowers himself onto it one joint at a time. He thinks about your question before he answers.

"House. Bar goes on at midnight, comes off at first light. That's now, near enough." He jerks his chin at the door. "I don't lift it in between. Not for the Fist, not for a man bleeding, not for my own sister, and she's tried. Anybody wants you in the night can knock till his knuckles go, and he can come back at breakfast."

He holds up a second finger.

"Callers by day wait down here. They don't go up my stair. Nobody does unless he's paid for the bed at the top of it. I come up and knock, and you come down or you don't. I don't say who's in the house. If someone asks, I say I keep an inn, not a list."

A third finger, and a sniff.

"Guild lads drink elsewhere. If one comes in polite, he gets told polite. If he comes in otherwise..." He looks at the poker against the hearthstones, and that's the rest of the sentence.

He watches the log burn for a moment.

"Somebody looking for you." It isn't a question. He looks at the crossbow propped by your knee, then at the cat under the window. "Most that come off a boat and say that are waiting on money or running from it. Don't tell me which. Just don't bring it through my door bleeding."

Then he pushes himself up off the stool, takes the poker, and goes to look at the bar across the door, though it hasn't moved. On the way back he stops beside your cat. It's still sitting under the shutter, face turned up to the slats on the lane side, and the tip of its tail is twitching.

"Yours wants out," Nantrin says. "There's a cat-flap in the scullery wall, low by the drain. Brick uses it. It's a cat's business where it goes at night, not mine." He puts the poker back in its place. "Room's top of the stair, at the back. Fire's laid. Bolt's on your side."

He goes behind the bar and starts wiping down a tap that's already clean. That's how an old man stays up without having to say he's waiting for you to finish.

The pottage is still warm, the log has caught properly, and the stair is there whenever you want it. Nothing else will happen tonight unless you want it to.

The cat is off the floor before you've finished the thought. It looks back at you once from the scullery doorway, and its tail goes straight up. Brick watches from under the bar with one yellow eye. When the flap knocks shut behind your cat, she shuts the eye again. Somebody else's cat using her door is not worth getting up for.

The link opens as easily as it did before.

The street comes up grey and sharp. The cat crosses it low and quick, past the Lady's niche. The candle stub has burned down another finger's width, and in the bowl your copper still stands on its edge against the far rim. The cat doesn't stop for it. It turns into the lane and goes along the wall side, the same way Tamsin told you to carry your purse.

The grate is about thirty paces in, ninety feet or so from where you're sitting by the hearth. The link is still clear there, but you can feel the far edge of it, the way you feel the end of a rope you're paying out. The Counting House waits at the end of the lane with its one hot yellow window, and that's farther than the bond reaches. The cat seems to know it. It stops at the grate and doesn't go a step past.

It puts its nose to the bars.

The cold air comes straight up into its face. Below the iron there is a shaft of old brick, square and slimed, dropping maybe fifteen feet. At the bottom, black water moves. It doesn't run like a drain. It lifts and settles, lifts and settles, slapping softly against the brick, slow as breathing. Salt, wet stone, and under them the old metal again, stronger here, like the smell left on your fingers from a purse of coppers that has been handled a long time.

Then there's something the cat didn't show you the first time. Just under the lip of the grate, an iron staple is driven into the brickwork, and a rope is tied to it. It's good hemp, tarred, knotted every arm's length. It hangs down the shaft and into the black water, and the end is under the surface. The cat's nose goes to it without being asked. Tar. Fish-oil. A man's sweat, sharp and fresh, a day or two old at most. Somebody has been down there, and he didn't take his rope up after him.

The pull doesn't come from the shaft, though. The cat makes that clear without having the words for it. The water at the bottom is only water. What it wants is beyond the water and below it, off to the side, toward the end of the lane where the Counting House stands. It's deep. *Wrong.* Under that *wrong*, the same hungry wanting as before. Its claws flex on the bars, and you feel how much it wants to slip between them. It doesn't. You told it not to.

Light comes swinging round the far end of the lane.

The cat is off the grate and flat in a doorway's shadow before you've registered the sound of boots. Two Flaming Fist men come up from the Counting House corner with a lantern on a pole, in red-and-orange, walking at the pace of men who have done this circuit too many times tonight. The lantern swings over the grate and doesn't stop there. Neither of them looks down.

"...twice an hour, and for what," one says. "Nobody's carrying a strongroom off through the gutter."

"Keep walking," says the other.

They pass the doorway within six feet. The cat's heart is going fast and light, and it doesn't move until the lantern has turned up Cheapside and gone. Then it creeps back to the grate's edge and sits there with its tail wrapped tight. The rope hangs in the shaft. The water breathes at the bottom.

It turns its head and looks back up the lane toward the Kegs. It's waiting for you.

At the hearth your own body sits with its eyes unfocused, and the log has burned down to half. Behind the bar, Nantrin has stopped wiping the tap.

The Lady's coin lies on James's palm, worn and warm from the cord against his chest. Her face on it is rubbed nearly smooth, like the stone one across the street. He speaks to it, and nothing answers. The candle flame stays upright. The coin stays a coin.

Nobody comes up the stair.

turns.message: I study the weeping face, searching my memory for a religious emblem like it—especially anything connected to Tymora or her darker sister, Beshaba.
turns.reply:
James turns the sheet a little in the Light, as if a different angle might make the woman lift her eyes. Some of it needs no searching. He has worn the Lady's coin for long enough, and prayed to her often enough, to know her signs. Tymora is the smiling woman, the silver disc, the coin flipped high. Her sister Beshaba, the Maid of Misfortune, takes black antlers on a red field for her sign. Her shrines are mostly an offering left at a crossroads so she'll look the other way, and nobody paints a face on that. Neither of them weeps. The rest is further back, in things half heard from temple-steps preachers and old priests across a dozen card tables.

It comes back to him on the second pass, and from somewhere he didn't expect: a wine-shop in Zazesspur in the last winter of the war. An old priest of the Lady was sitting with soldiers who had a few days to live, or thought they had, and he was paying for his drink in stories. James was nineteen and losing at bones, and he listened with half an ear.

Before there were two sisters, the old man said, there was one. Her name was Tyche, and she was all of luck, the good and the bad, in one woman. In the oldest days something rotted her. The priest named Moander, the rotting god, and said Lathander had a hand in the breaking, and he lowered his voice for that part. She split in two. The fair half became Tymora and the foul half became Beshaba, and they have hated each other ever since, the way only family can. Then the priest took a coin from his purse, a southern bronze so old it was nearly black, with a woman's face on both sides. One face smiled. The other wept. *That's her as she was,* he said. *Both of them, one coin. Whichever face lies up is the one that's ruling.* Then he flipped it and caught it and showed the soldiers the smile, and James never learned whether he'd cheated.

The face in Vane's paper is that face. She has a rim like a coin and a ring of letters too fine to read, and she is weeping. She isn't Beshaba's sign, since the Maid has never needed a face to be feared. She is the other side of the Lady's coin, the side that should lie face down.

One part of the memory doesn't fit what he's looking at. The priest's coin was a curiosity, something from a temple's back shelf. A rich house's paper-mark is the house's own badge, cut into the mould once and kept for generations. Somebody made a patriar house's paper carry the old double goddess. And of her two faces, this paper shows the weeping one.

The cat on the stool hasn't turned around. Its tail has come loose from its feet, and the tip twitches once, then again.

Downstairs, Nantrin's voice comes up the stairwell, dry and not loud: "Bacon won't wait on a man reading." The Light burns steady on Tymora's coin. Nothing else needs James until he goes down, unless he wants it to.

At the corner of the side lane it stops for a moment and looks down towards the pale bulk of the Counting House. By day the place is all open shutters and clerks on the steps. Then it turns and comes on without being called.

At the bottom of Cheapside a crier in a stained blue coat is standing on a mounting block with a bundle of broadsheets under one arm. He's shouting the same lines over and over to anyone who'll slow down.

"*Baldur's Mouth!* Third this season! Drowned man off the Grey Harbour steps at dawn, and a copper in his teeth! Umberlee's sisters say it's no offering of theirs! The Fist says it's no murder of theirs! *Baldur's Mouth*, two copper, read who's paying the sea!"

A couple of dockmen buy a sheet and argue over it as they walk off. One of them says the sea takes what it's owed. The other says the sea doesn't pay coppers, people do.

East along the inside of the outer wall the crowd thins. There are fewer stalls and more warehouses here, and the air smells of dung and hot iron instead of fish. The Basilisk Gate is just as Nantrin described it: a deep, dark arch with a stone lizard crouched over it. Half its head and one foreleg have broken away, so it looks more like a sleeping dog than a basilisk. Two Flaming Fist men on the gate are going through a farmer's turnip cart for no reason anyone can see. One of them glances at James's crossbow and then at the cat, decides neither is a turnip, and waves him through with two fingers.

Outside the wall the city doesn't stop. It just stops being tidy. The road out from the gate is mud and straw, lined on both sides by fenced yards full of wagons, axle-trees, mules and men shouting about axles. James asks the first carter he sees for Hesk's. The man points with his whip, three yards along on the left, and adds without being asked, "Tell her I'll have it Highharvestide."

Hesk's yard has a painted board over the gate, HESK — CARTAGE — BREWERS & GENERAL, and the paint is newer than the board. Inside is a packed-earth yard with two big drays and a lighter wagon, a long stable along one side with mules' heads looking out over the half-doors, and a house of whitewashed brick at the back. A tall, heavy-shouldered woman of about fifty stands in the middle of it with her sleeves rolled to the elbow and a slate in one hand. She is telling a young drayman exactly how much a cracked barrel costs and who will be paying for it.

"...six silver for the cask, and the beer's on top, and it's coming out of yours, not mine." She looks up at James, takes in the cloak, the crossbow and the cat in one sweep, and goes straight to business. "If you're hiring, the light wagon's free from noon. If you're owing, you're early, and I'll take it."

Before James can answer, a voice comes from the stable, slow and low, plainly talking to a mule. "No, you don't. Stand. *Stand.* There's a good lass."

A man ducks out under the half-door with a hoof-pick in his hand. He's lean and bandy-legged, somewhere past fifty, with a grey beard cropped short and a face the road has turned to leather. He's wiping his hands down his apron when he sees James, and his hands stop.

Dace Rook looks at him for a long moment. He looks at James's face, then at his hands, then at the cat. Then he looks back at the hands again.

"Well," he says. "Corra said you'd turn up if you were ever this far north." He doesn't come any closer yet. The hoof-pick hangs from his fingers. "You come to eat, James, or you come for your money?"

Orla Hesk has stopped talking to the drayman. She's watching the two of them over her slate.

note.text:
The strongest part was the atmosphere. The quay, Nantrin’s inn, and Hesk’s yard felt inhabited rather than staged for James. Tamsin’s nervous politeness, Brannick’s guarded professionalism, and Nantrin’s firm house rules gave me people I wanted to talk to. Corra’s letter was the highlight: affectionate, practical, and gently damning about James’s gambling. It gave me a reason to visit Dace beyond collecting money.

The cat worked very well as a patron’s instrument. Its conflicting attraction and fear made the Counting House intriguing without simply delivering instructions. Scouting the grate produced useful facts—distance, rope, water, patrol—while respecting the limit I set. That felt like information I could eventually build a plan around.

**What broke**
- The starting records weren’t reconciled with the campaign files. The missing letter interrupted a good scene, especially when I was initially asked to invent something explicitly left to the GM. The correction was gracious, and the resulting letter was excellent.
- There were other sheet discrepancies: Arcana became History, the rapier lost its established proficiency, and the rod and cloak required attunement despite the campaign override. These didn’t affect a roll today, but they undermine confidence in later mechanical play.
- One combined out-of-game correction and in-character action returned “The question could not be sent.” I can’t diagnose that, but it broke the flow.

**What was missing**
A little more momentum and room for initiative from NPCs. I enjoyed choosing to visit Dace, but many turns ended with some version of “nothing else will happen unless you want it to.” Repeated that often, it made the city feel less independent than the descriptions suggested. Likewise, reminders that breakfast was waiting started to feel like nudges to stop investigating.

The mystery has strong ingredients, but I’m ready for an actionable proposition soon: someone who wants something, an opportunity with a deadline, or a concrete lead James can pursue. Not the big reveal yet—just enough to begin making consequential choices toward the crew-and-heist campaign.

Overall, I wanted to keep playing. Preserve the character work and careful scouting, clean up the records, and let the world push back a little more.

But Nantrin had just explained that the inn was barred for the night, and the cat felt both drawn to and frightened by something below. I chose not to turn a first look into a solo dungeon entry.

That restraint felt good: I had discovered a possible approach worth returning to with preparation.

There was also a smaller moment with Tamsin. I wanted to press him about the lit window, but James had explicitly offered him permission not to answer. When he dodged, I let him go. I’m still curious whether someone he cares about works there.

opening.text:
The gangplank bounces once under your boots, and then there is stone — the Lower City quay of Baldur's Gate, slick with harbour damp and loud with the end of a working day. Lanterns are coming alight along the waterfront one by one. Porters shout, a barge horn groans somewhere on the Chionthar, and above it all the city climbs in a jumble of roofs towards the dark line of the inner wall.

The cat lands beside you, tail high, and studies the quay as if it had been told to expect something.

Ahead, the passengers from your ship shuffle into a line before a trestle table under a Flaming Fist awning. A broad sergeant with an ink-stained thumb looks up from his ledger at each face. "Name. Business in the Gate. Where you'll sleep," he says, over and over, without much patience left in his voice.

To your left, on an upturned barrel by a warehouse door, a woman with quick hands fans a deck of cards. The sailors around her groan and laugh as a hand goes the wrong way. "One more seat, friend," she calls, and her eyes find you. "You look like someone who knows how to read a table."

A thin tiefling lad with a rope sling over his shoulder slips along the queue. "Carry your things up to the Lower City, ser? Cheap. Know every inn worth the name." A merchant ahead of you pulls his purse closer and steps away from him.

You have about three hundred and fifty gold, a promissory note from a man who lost the same night you won, and an order from a goddess who did not say how you would learn what she wants of you. The line moves forward. The sergeant's pen is waiting, the cards are being shuffled again, and the porter is already looking your way.
